title: Verifying cited answers: signed manifests, content hashes and ledger evidence
abstract: An independent verification workflow for a cited answer against ledger evidence, with a distinction between cryptographic consistency and validated settlement.
body:
Verification of a cited answer begins with the exported receipt bundle rather than the displayed summary. Each citation binds an article identifier, version and exact passage identifier. The cited text must occur in the delivered body. A paid citation additionally needs a verified grant associated with the successful purchase intent. A preview is discovery metadata and cannot supply premium evidence merely because its wording sounds relevant.

The signed manifest binds the writer wallet, article version, price and passage root. A signature is useful only if its signing key derives to the registered seller wallet. The buyer checks that relationship before considering a paid search hit. Otherwise an attacker could attach a valid signature from an unrelated key and borrow the reputation of a different writer. This is an identity binding check rather than an editorial assessment.

Passage verification uses salted hashes committed under a manifest root. After authorized delivery, the receipt supplies the passages and salts needed to recompute those commitments. An independent verifier checks exact text rather than a plausible paraphrase. The answer can summarize the passage, but its citation must still resolve to the authenticated delivered bytes. Invalid citations are withheld instead of silently repaired with unrelated material.

Key reveal adds another verification layer. The signed quote commits to the encrypted envelope, plaintext hash, initialization vector, authentication tag and hash condition. The finish publishes a key whose preimage binding must match that condition. The verifier authenticates and decrypts the envelope, checks the delivered identity, and validates the passage commitments. A successful offline check proves internal consistency of these objects; it does not independently prove that the ledger accepted the transaction.

To establish ledger finality, query the named Testnet transaction hashes and require successful validated results. Match the create and finish to the intended buyer, seller, amount and escrow object. For issued-token escrow, check the correct issuer and currency and the exact balance delta. The requested transaction amount alone is insufficient evidence of what arrived. An answer anchor separately binds the recorded audit head to a ledger transaction.

Endpoint history is an operational dependency. A transaction not found on one public server may be available from another approved history endpoint. That response is an availability result, not proof of a failed purchase. Retain hashes and ledger indexes in evidence reports, record the endpoint used, and keep unresolved checks visible. Testnet resets can remove historical data, so an old successful local verification is not a guarantee that future public lookup will work.

Identity Credentials answer a separate question. An accepted, unexpired credential from a trusted issuer supports an identity attestation. It does not prove article accuracy, independent authorship, market adoption or production readiness. A receipt reader should preserve both the identity status and the content provenance rather than interpreting either as an endorsement of every claim.

Keep private credentials outside this workflow. Wallet seeds and API tokens are unnecessary for read-only receipt verification and must not be placed in prompts, logs or published evidence. Published fulfillment keys are different: after settlement they are intentionally public and may be needed to verify the encrypted delivery. That public key reveal is not permission to expose a wallet signing key, and it does not unlock another buyer copy encrypted under a fresh key.
